title: Episode 207: The Persian Empire: Queen Esther, Xerxes, and the Deliverance of Purim
description:
Inside the winter palace of Susa, King Ahasuerus—identified as the mighty Persian Emperor Xerxes I—ruled an empire spanning one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. Following the banishment of Queen Vashti, a beautiful young Hebrew orphan named Hadassah, raised by her cousin Mordecai and taking the Persian name Esther, was chosen as the new Queen of Persia, keeping her Jewish heritage secret. When royal grand vizier Haman the Agagite became enraged by Mordecai's refusal to bow, he manipulated Xerxes into issuing a genocidal decree ordering the extermination of every Jewish man, woman, and child across the empire on a single date determined by casting lots, or Purim. Facing lethal danger, Mordecai challenged the young queen: 'Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' Risking execution under the Persian law that decreed death for anyone entering the inner throne room uninvited, Esther approached the golden scepter, exposing Haman's plot and turning the tables of history. Discover the royal drama, courage, and celebration of Purim.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our Persian Empire saga with an unforgettable drama of court intrigue, hidden identity, and extraordinary courage in the Citadel of Susa. Here is George with the story of Queen Esther, Xerxes, and the deliverance of Purim.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE OPULENT FEAST OF KING XERXES
In 483 BC, King Ahasuerus—known to Greek historians and modern archaeology as Xerxes I—reigned supreme over the Persian Empire from his winter capital at Susa. Preparing to launch his colossal military invasion of mainland Greece with hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of ships, Xerxes hosted a spectacular, six-month festival for his satraps, generals, and nobles to display the staggering wealth and military splendor of his kingdom. The celebration culminated in a seven-day public feast in the palace gardens: under white, green, and blue linen awnings fastened with purple cords to silver rings and marble pillars, guests reclined on couches of gold and silver set upon pavements of porphyry, mother-of-pearl, and turquoise stone. Royal wine flowed without restriction from golden goblets, each of unique design. On the final day, merry with wine, Xerxes commanded his royal eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before the banquet wearing her royal crown, to show off her beauty to the intoxicated assembly. Vashti boldly refused the humiliating command. Enraged, Xerxes consulted his legal counselors, who warned that Vashti's defiance would inspire wives across the empire to despise their husbands. Vashti was banished from the royal presence, and a search began for a new queen. King Xerxes's opulent palace at Susa was adorned with dazzling glazed brick reliefs of winged bulls, griffin lions, and Persian spearmen, excavated by French archaeologists in the nineteenth century, confirming the biblical descriptions of royal luxury in vivid detail.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: HADASSAH AT THE CITADEL: THE SECRET QUEEN
Royal officers combed the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the empire, bringing the most beautiful young maidens to the palace harem in Susa. Among them was an orphaned Jewish maiden named Hadassah—meaning 'Myrtle'—who had been raised with tender devotion by her cousin Mordecai, a palace official descended from the tribe of Benjamin. Mordecai instructed her to conceal her Jewish identity, giving her the Persian name Esther, derived from the word for 'Star' or the goddess Ishtar. For twelve months, Esther underwent royal purification treatments—six months with sweet oil of myrrh and six months with fragrant spices and perfumes—under the care of Hegai, keeper of the women. Unlike other candidates who demanded elaborate jewels, Esther asked only for what Hegai advised, winning the admiration of everyone who saw her. When Esther was brought into the presence of King Xerxes in the seventh year of his reign, the King was captivated by her beauty, grace, and humble dignity. Setting the royal crown upon her head, Xerxes proclaimed Esther Queen of Persia, declaring a nationwide holiday and distributing royal gifts, unaware that his new bride belonged to the people of the covenant. Hadassah's secret Hebrew identity was preserved through strict discipline and the prudent advice of Mordecai. Her elevation to Queen of Persia demonstrated how divine providence works quietly behind palace corridors to position key individuals for historic moments of deliverance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: MORDECAI AT THE KING'S GATE
While Esther lived in the splendor of the palace, Mordecai sat daily at the King's Gate, keeping watch over her welfare. While on duty, Mordecai overheard two royal eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, plotting an assassination against King Xerxes. Mordecai immediately relayed the plot to Queen Esther, who informed the King in Mordecai's name. An investigation confirmed the conspiracy; the two traitors were hanged on the gallows, and the heroic act of Mordecai was recorded in the official Royal Book of Chronicles in the King's presence, though Mordecai received no immediate reward. Shortly thereafter, Xerxes promoted a wealthy nobleman named Haman the Agagite—a descendant of the ancient Amalekite kings who had been sworn enemies of Israel—to the supreme office of Grand Vizier. The King commanded that all royal servants at the King's Gate bow down and pay homage to Haman whenever he passed. Thousands prostrated themselves in the dust, but Mordecai stood tall, refusing to bow to an Amalekite. Filled with burning rage, Haman decided that executing Mordecai alone was insufficient: he resolved to exterminate every single Jewish citizen living throughout the entire Persian Empire. Mordecai's refusal to bow to Haman was rooted in deep spiritual conviction. As an Agagite descendant of the Amalekite kings, Haman represented the ancient enemies of Israel, making homage a profound moral compromise that Mordecai would not permit.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CASTING OF PURIM AND THE ROYAL DECREE
In the twelfth year of Xerxes's reign, in the first month of Nisan, Haman cast the 'Pur'—the lot—before his astrologers to determine the luckiest day to execute his genocidal scheme. The lot fell on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, giving eleven months to mobilize the empire. Haman approached King Xerxes with a deceitful, xenophobic argument: 'There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king's laws: therefore it is not for the king's profit to suffer them.' Haman offered to pay ten thousand talents of silver—equivalent to two-thirds of the annual imperial revenue—into the royal treasury to finance the slaughter. Xerxes removed his signet ring, handed it to Haman, and said: 'The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee.' Royal scribes drafted the edict, sealed with the King's ring, commanding that on the thirteenth of Adar, all Jews—young and old, women and children—be destroyed, killed, and annihilated, and their property plundered as spoil. Dispatched by royal couriers, the decree threw the empire into mourning. Haman's casting of the Pur was an appeal to pagan astrology and omens to choose the most auspicious time for genocide. Yet the eleven-month delay between the casting of lots and the appointed day of execution provided the exact window needed for deliverance to unfold.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: 'FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS'
When Mordecai learned of the decree, he tore his clothes, put on coarse sackcloth and ashes, and walked through the center of Susa wailing with a loud and bitter cry. When Queen Esther heard of Mordecai's grief, she sent garments to clothe him, but he refused. Mordecai delivered a copy of the genocidal decree to Esther through her eunuch Hathach, commanding her to go to the King and beg for mercy for her people. Esther hesitated, reminding Mordecai of the unyielding law of the Medes and Persians: any person, man or woman, who entered the inner court to the King without being summoned was subject to instant execution, unless the King held out the golden scepter to spare their life, and she had not been called for thirty days. Mordecai answered with words that echoed through Jewish history: 'Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews. For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' Mordecai's impassioned appeal to Esther underscored the profound truth of personal responsibility in the face of injustice. Silence in the presence of evil was complicity; courage in the face of mortal peril was the only path of honor and salvation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SCEPTER EXTENDED AND THE SLEEPLESS NIGHT
Esther's courage crystallized. She commanded Mordecai to gather all the Jews in Susa to fast with her for three days and nights, taking neither food nor water: 'I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.' On the third day, Esther dressed in royal robes and stepped into the inner courtyard opposite the royal throne room. Xerxes looked up and saw his young queen standing in silent peril. Moved to deep compassion, the King extended the golden scepter in his hand. Esther stepped forward and touched the top of the scepter. 'What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.' With masterly tactical restraint, Esther invited the King and Haman to an intimate banquet of wine that evening, and then to a second banquet the following night. That night, God took sleep from Xerxes. Troubled by insomnia, the King commanded the Royal Chronicles to be read aloud. By divine providence, the scribe read the neglected account of Mordecai uncovering the assassination plot, prompting Xerxes to realize that the man who saved his life had never been honored. Esther's fast of three days and nights united the entire Jewish community of Susa in collective prayer. When she stepped unsummoned into the inner court, her royal composure masked a heart surrendered entirely to divine will, risking life for her people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GALLOWS OF HAMAN AND THE FEAST OF PURIM
At that moment, Haman entered the outer court to ask the King's permission to hang Mordecai on a seventy-five-foot gallows he had erected. Before Haman could speak, Xerxes asked: 'What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour?' Thinking the King meant him, Haman proposed royal robes worn by the King, the royal horse, and a crown, paraded through the city. Xerxes commanded: 'Make haste, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew!' In humiliating agony, Haman led his mortal enemy through the streets of Susa. That evening at Esther's second banquet, the Queen exposed the murderous plot: 'We are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish!' Xerxes raged: 'Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?' Esther pointed her finger: 'The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman!' Terrified, Haman fell upon Esther's couch begging for life, but Xerxes ordered him hanged upon the very gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. Mordecai was elevated to Grand Vizier, a counter-decree was issued allowing the Jews to arm and defend themselves, and on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, the Jewish people celebrated their deliverance, instituting the joyous annual festival of Purim. The establishment of the annual festival of Purim remains one of the most joyous celebrations in Jewish tradition. Through costume, feasting, charity to the poor, and reading the Megillah, generations remember how an orphaned queen and a loyal official overturned imperial doom.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Through Esther's courage, the Jewish people survived the wrath of Persia, preserving the lineage of Abraham in the Middle East. But across the Aegean Sea, a tempest was gathering in the mountains of Macedonia that would sweep away the Persian Empire forever. Next week, we begin our Greek and Seleucid saga with Episode 208: Alexander the Great, the Phalanx, and the Hellenization of the East: Philip's phalanx, Bucephalus, the Battle of Issus, the seven-month siege of Tyre, Alexander's peaceful march to the Temple of Jerusalem, and the founding of Alexandria. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
